text: What we built during the Global Energy Hackathon: GridRescue AI, decision-support software for hospitals on weak grids. A grid mapper that reads any site from open data. A relocation plan that answers the brief's five questions. An hour-by-hour outage simulation, with a machine-learning classification of the energy system. And an ESG report. The case: the National Orthopaedic Hospital, Enugu: about six hours of grid a day, a theatre that waits for the generator, and a move in five years. Here is one hospital, end to end.
Step one, the pin drop. The pin sits at Abakpa Junction, Enugu, and GridRescue reads the site.

Step two, the site read. Five point four eight peak-sun hours a day, from NASA POWER, P V G I S, PVWatts and the Global Solar Atlas. Nine substations within fifty kilometres, from OpenStreetMap; yet six hours of supply a day, as the hospital's head engineer reports; our grid read: class D, poor. The published tariff: one hundred and sixty naira per kilowatt hour.

The hospital must move, so we switch on hospital is moving. The new-site lens scores areas within twelve kilometres on grid access and distance. The best is four kilometres north, with a substation one point three kilometres away. We pick it, and lock the site.

The relocation plan answers the brief's five questions: which loads must never lose power, how the system moves, who owns it, whether diesel savings repay it, and which funders have backed similar projects.

Step three, the outage simulation, in three D on the hospital's own site. At six in the evening the grid drops. The online U P S switches the theatres in zero milliseconds, modelled; the energy containers carry the theatres, I C U and burns through the night; the generator stays last.

Step four, the recommended design. Best for this site: ground-mounted solar, one thousand six hundred and seventy kilowatts peak; a containerised energy system, five thousand kilowatt hours; the theatre U P S; and the existing generator, last. The machine-learning classifier, trained on synthetic sites, picks this energy system at seventy-six percent; the hourly simulation makes the final call.

Four outage cases are tested: the twelve-hour design outage, a twenty-four-hour national grid collapse, the worst solar month, and an eighteen-hour outage. All four covered, one hundred percent of the critical load in the model. This is the national collapse.

Step five, cost and payback. No upfront capital: an energy service company owns the system and charges sixty-nine million naira a month, against about three hundred million of modelled diesel. Bought outright instead, diesel savings repay the system and the move in one point six years. Over ten years: thirty-seven point six billion naira on diesel, fifteen point nine billion on the service. The funders are named.

Step six, the results, before and after. Theatre-hours without grid power: four thousand nine hundred and ninety-two a year today, zero on the system. Diesel for the protected load: about 1.04 million litres a year, down to about 176 thousand. Energy cost of the protected load, year one: 3.8 billion naira to 1.6 billion. Carbon dioxide: 2,795 tonnes a year to 549; two thousand two hundred and forty-six tonnes avoided, net.

The ESG report, one click, for the board: Scope one, the diesel no longer burnt; Scope two, the grid power bought, netted off; environment, social and governance lines; and carbon credits valued only after verification.

Every number is a modelled engine result, to be confirmed with the hospital's load audit and fuel logs. One simulation covers every outage type: grid load-shedding, transmission and substation failures, severe weather and diesel shortages are tested today. Next come area-based outages, from one feeder to a district or a whole state, and cybersecurity outages that cut the grid, communication or control, as further stress scenarios. Hospitals and health networks pay GridRescue for the assessment and an annual licence; any pin on the map works, so it scales to every critical facility. GridRescue AI turns energy planning into investment-ready decisions. We start with hospitals, where power is life, and grow to every critical facility. Map the grid. Keep the theatres on. Move with the hospital.
